transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it’s this business with bridges. I mean, I’ve been around a long time, driven plenty of places, and you’d think at my age I’d be past getting rattled by things. But if I know I have to cross a bridge—before I’m even on it—my heart starts pounding, and my hands get damp on the steering wheel or the armrest if I’m not the one driving.

It’s a terrible rush of fear, just all at once. Funny, I can sit and talk about other things—my old job, my grandchildren, whatever—but the moment a bridge crossing becomes unavoidable, that fear just takes over.
Is it just bridges that trigger this fear, or are there other types of situations or places that cause a similar reaction?

It’s really the bridges—especially those high ones, the big spans. I know, rationally, thousands of cars go over them every day. I’m not foolish about that. But when I see one on the map, or coming up through the windshield, it feels like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away underneath us.

I suppose other things can make a person uneasy—my brother never liked elevators, funny enough—but for me, it’s that bridge feeling. That height, that span ahead. That’s what sets me off.
Does your fear occur only when you are about to cross a bridge, or do you also experience it in other high places, such as tall buildings or mountain edges?

Well, I suppose I’m not thrilled with heights in general, but it’s really the bridge that does it—the high span, you know. I can know perfectly well that thousands of cars go over those bridges every day, just like I know my grandson’s phone has more power than the computers they used to put men on the moon—he’s always telling me that—but when I see one coming up through the windshield, or even just notice it on a map, it feels like the whole thing is waiting to drop away underneath us. That’s the part that grabs me.
Does seeing a bridge, even from a distance or in a picture, trigger your fear?

Yes, even seeing it from a distance can start it up—especially if it’s one of those high spans. A picture, or on a map, or coming up ahead through the windshield… I know full well cars go over those bridges all day long. I’m not saying it makes sense.

But in that moment it feels like the whole thing is just waiting to give way underneath us. Funny, my grandson showed me one of those satellite map things once—amazing what they can do now—but if I spot the bridge on there, I can feel myself tense up before I’m anywhere near it.
Does your fear of bridges occur only when you're driving across them, or does it also happen when you're walking or being driven across?

It’s not only when I’m the one driving, no. If the crossing becomes unavoidable—whether I’m behind the wheel or just sitting there being driven—my heart starts pounding before we’re even on it. My hands get damp, either on the steering wheel or gripping the armrest.

Walking across… I try not to put myself in that position, to be honest. I remember years ago they used to talk about scenic walkways and all that, and my wife loved a view—she could stand there admiring the water like it was a postcard—but for me, once it’s clear I have to cross, that terrible rush of fear comes up right away. It’s the being committed to the bridge, I suppose, more than the particular way I’m crossing it.
Does thinking about a bridge, without seeing it, trigger your fear?

Thinking about it alone… yes, sometimes. Not every stray thought, mind you—I can think of the word “bridge” if we’re talking about cards or something, though I never learned bridge properly, my brother did—but if I picture one of those high spans, or remember it on a map, then it starts to feel real.

I know perfectly well thousands of cars cross them every day, but in my mind it’s like I can see it ahead through the windshield, and it feels as if the whole thing is just waiting to drop away under us.
Does your fear occur when you are in a high place, but not necessarily on a bridge, such as at the top of a tall building or a mountain?

I’m not sure I can say, Doctor. I don’t really go up tall buildings much anymore, and mountains—well, my knees wouldn’t thank me for that, even if the rest of me wanted to.

I suppose heights can make a person uneasy, can’t they? My wife used to love those lookout points, always wanted a photograph, and I’d be the one holding the camera crooked. But whether that’s the same fear as the bridge thing… I don’t know. I haven’t really noticed it in the same clear way.
Do you experience a similar level of fear when you are in a high place but not moving, such as standing at the edge of a cliff or at the top of a tall building?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t spend much time at the edges of cliffs—at my age, even a curb can feel like something to pay attention to if the pavement’s uneven.

Tall buildings, I suppose I’ve been in them now and then, hospitals and offices and the like, but I don’t usually go right up to the glass and look down. My wife used to do that—she’d say, “Come see the view,” and I’d say I could see perfectly well from where I was. But whether that was the same kind of fear, the same level… I can’t say I’ve noticed it clearly. It’s not something I’ve tested much.
Would your fear be less intense if you were on a very high bridge that did not span a body of water, such as a bridge over a wide valley?

I don’t know that the water is the main thing, really. I mean, water makes it look worse sometimes—my wife used to say I shouldn’t stare down, which is easy advice to give when you’re not the one looking.

But if it’s a high span, even over a valley, I think it would still get me. I can know, in my sensible head, that cars go over those bridges all day long. But if I see it ahead of us, or even see it marked on the map and know we’re coming to it, it starts to feel like the whole bridge is just… waiting to drop away underneath. So no, I’m not sure it would be much less intense just because there wasn’t water.
Would you feel a similar level of fear if you were on a very high observation deck or platform that wasn't a bridge?

I don’t really know, Doctor. I haven’t been on one of those high observation decks in a long time, if ever in the sort of way you mean.

My wife and I did go to places with views sometimes—she liked views, always did—but I tended to stay back a bit, look at the plaques or the gift shop, you know. They always have those little racks of postcards and magnets, and half the time the photograph is better than what you can see through the haze anyway.

So… would it be the same level of fear? I can’t say for certain. I imagine I wouldn’t be eager to stand right out on some platform and look down, but I don’t have a clear example like I do with bridges.
Would you feel a similar level of fear if you were in a very high, enclosed space like a tall elevator?

I’m not really sure about that one. Elevators… well, I’ve been in plenty of elevators, of course—doctor’s offices, hospitals, those parking garages where you can never remember whether you left the car on level C or level 3. My wife used to have a better memory for that sort of thing.

But a tall elevator, enclosed like that, I don’t know. If I can’t see out, I’m not sure it would strike me the same way. I suppose if somebody told me, “We’re going up fifty floors,” I might think about it, but I don’t have a clear memory of being frightened in that situation the way I do with certain bridges.
Would you feel afraid in a very high, enclosed space like the top floor of a skyscraper with no outdoor access?

I don’t know that I can give you a clean answer on that. If it’s all enclosed, no balcony or outside bit, I might not even think about the height unless someone made a point of it.

I remember being in office buildings years ago—well, not skyscrapers exactly, more the kind with too many identical hallways and those fluorescent lights that make everyone look tired. My wife used to say I walked too fast in places like that, but I think I was just trying to find the right door before I forgot why we were there.

So, top floor with no outdoor access… I’m not sure. Maybe if there were huge windows and I could really see straight down, I might not like that. But I don’t have a definite example where I know I’d feel the same fear as on a bridge.
Is your fear of bridges more about the act of crossing over the bridge, or is it primarily about being in a high place?

It’s more the bridge itself, I think—the crossing, yes, but especially when it’s one of those high spans. I can know in my head that thousands of cars go over it every day, trucks too, and nothing happens. I mean, they wouldn’t build the thing if it wasn’t meant to hold traffic.

But then I see it coming up through the windshield, or even notice it on the map ahead of time, and it feels… not reasonable, but it feels like the whole bridge is just waiting to drop away underneath us. Like the road won’t stay a road.

High places may be part of it, I suppose, but bridges have their own feeling to me. They’re different.
Would your fear be triggered by standing on a high, narrow walkway with no handrail, even if it's not a bridge?

I’m not sure, doctor. A high narrow walkway with no handrail… that sounds unpleasant just hearing it, but I don’t know that I’ve actually been in that exact situation.

I remember once at a museum they had one of those little raised platforms—though it had rails, I think. Or maybe that was the train station, now that I’m thinking of it. My wife always liked reading all the signs, and I’d be halfway through the room before realizing she’d stopped behind me.

But no handrail, high up… I suppose I wouldn’t be eager to stand there. I just can’t say for certain whether it would hit me the same way a bridge does.
Would you say your fear is more about the height of the bridge or the fact that it's a bridge itself?

I think it’s the bridge itself, though the height makes it worse. It’s funny, I can sit here and know perfectly well that thousands of cars cross those bridges every day. They’re engineered for it, inspected, all that.

But then if I see a high span marked on the map, or it comes into view through the windshield, my mind doesn’t stay with all that sensible information. It’s like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away underneath us. Not every high place gives me that same feeling, but a bridge does.
Would you feel afraid standing on a wide, flat, elevated surface with a secure fence or wall around it, such as a rooftop garden?

A rooftop garden… with a good fence around it? I don’t know that it would do the same thing to me. I mean, I might notice I’m up high, but that’s not quite the feeling.

With bridges, it’s different. I can know perfectly well that thousands of cars go across them every day, but when I see one of those high spans coming up on the map or through the windshield, it feels like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away under us. A flat roof with a wall around it doesn’t quite have that same… road-over-empty-space feeling.
Would you feel afraid in a high, enclosed space like an airplane during flight?

An airplane… I can’t say that’s been the same thing for me, doctor. I mean, I haven’t really sorted it out that way.

Once you’re inside, it’s all enclosed, isn’t it? Little windows, seats, people fussing with bags overhead—my wife used to always pack too much for a trip, and then I’d be the one trying to wedge it into the bin while everyone waited behind me. Funny what you remember.

But as to being high up in the air… I’m not sure I’ve noticed that same feeling like with a bridge. I’d have to think about it more.
Would you feel afraid standing near the edge of a wide, open staircase with no railing or wall to block your view of the drop below?

A staircase with no railing… well, I suppose I wouldn’t like being near the edge much. Anyone would be careful there, wouldn’t they?

But the thing I keep coming back to is the bridge. I know, sitting here, that thousands of cars go over those bridges every day and nothing happens. But if I see a high span on the map, or it comes into view through the windshield, it just feels like the whole thing is waiting to drop away underneath us. It’s not quite just “looking down,” if that makes sense.
Would you feel afraid on a wide, flat bridge with high sides or walls that prevent seeing down?

Even if I couldn’t see straight down… yes, I think the bridge itself would still get to me. It’s that high span, you know? I can tell myself perfectly well that thousands of cars go over it every day, back and forth, and nothing happens.

But when it shows up on the map, or I see it ahead through the windshield, my mind goes right to this feeling that the whole thing is just waiting to drop away under us. The walls might help with the view, maybe, but it’s still a bridge.
Would you feel afraid on a bridge with a solid floor and walls that prevent seeing down, if you knew you were high above the ground?

Yes… yes, I think so. Even if I couldn’t see down, if I knew it was one of those high bridges, that would be enough.

I know perfectly well cars go over them all day long—thousands of them—and nothing happens. My son used to say, “Dad, it’s built for this,” which of course it is. Engineers and all that. But if I see that high span on the map, or coming up through the windshield, it’s like my mind decides the whole thing is just waiting to drop away underneath us. The walls wouldn’t really change that part.

A rooftop garden… with a good fence around it? I don’t know that it would do the same thing to me. I mean, I might notice I’m up high, but that’s not quite the feeling.

With bridges, it’s different. I can know perfectly well that thousands of cars go across them every day, but when I see one of those high spans coming up on the map or through the windshield, it feels like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away under us. A flat roof with a wall around it doesn’t quite have that same… road-over-empty-space feeling.

An airplane… I can’t say that’s been the same thing for me, doctor. I mean, I haven’t really sorted it out that way.

Once you’re inside, it’s all enclosed, isn’t it? Little windows, seats, people fussing with bags overhead—my wife used to always pack too much for a trip, and then I’d be the one trying to wedge it into the bin while everyone waited behind me. Funny what you remember.

But as to being high up in the air… I’m not sure I’ve noticed that same feeling like with a bridge. I’d have to think about it more.

A staircase with no railing… well, I suppose I wouldn’t like being near the edge much. Anyone would be careful there, wouldn’t they?

But the thing I keep coming back to is the bridge. I know, sitting here, that thousands of cars go over those bridges every day and nothing happens. Even if I couldn’t see straight down… yes, I think the bridge itself would still get to me. It’s that high span, you know? I can tell myself perfectly well that thousands of cars go over it every day, back and forth, and nothing happens.
